query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor silver addition (≈2–3 at.%) into the CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy will trigger in situ formation of a self‐adaptive, lubricious oxide nanocomposite surface during sliding that maintains low friction and wear across the entire temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk single‐phase CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy matrix with its native microstructure.
generation.intervention: Alloying the CoCrFeNi base with approximately 2–3 atomic percent silver.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed in ambient air under constant normal load (e.g., ~5 N) and controlled sliding speed, with the temperature varied from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an in situ, deformable oxide nanocomposite tribolayer in which finely dispersed Ag nanocrystals are embedded in an amorphous oxide matrix.
generation.mechanism: The silver acts as a reactive element that catalyzes tribochemical reactions during sliding. At elevated temperatures, it promotes the nucleation and growth of a continuous, strong yet lubricious oxide scale that adapts to damage by dynamically healing minor wear features. This dual action suppresses adhesive and oxidative wear both at low and high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the pure CoCrFeNi alloy, the Ag-alloyed variant will show a significantly lower and more stable coefficient of friction (e.g., approaching or below 0.1 under high-temperature sliding) and exhibit wear rates reduced by up to one or two orders of magnitude across the full temperature range.
generation.baseline: The unalloyed CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy, which tends to exhibit increased friction and wear at higher temperatures due to less effective tribochemical surface adaptation.
generation.boundary: This beneficial effect is expected during sliding in ambient air under moderate loads and may not hold in inert atmospheres or under extreme loads/environmental conditions. Additionally, excessive silver content might lead to deleterious segregation, so the effect is constrained to low-level additions.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extrapolates the reactive wear protection behavior observed in systems such as (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (PMC8448869) and adaptive nanocomposite surface formation in NiX alloys (PMC10241162::web::000::abstract) to the CoCrFeNi matrix. While the role of Ag in catalyzing protective oxide layer formation is promising, the exact distribution of Ag in the CoCrFeNi matrix and the detailed tribochemical pathways remain to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using identical processing for (a) pure CoCrFeNi and (b) CoCrFeNi with 2–3 at.% Ag. Perform ball‐on‐disk sliding tests in ambient air under identical load and sliding speed conditions at several temperatures (e.g., RT, 300 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C). Characterize the friction coefficient in real time and measure wear volumes through profilometry. Additionally, use SEM/TEM and energy dispersive spectroscopy to examine the wear tracks and identify the formation and continuity of the oxide nanocomposite surface layer.
measurements: Friction coefficient vs. sliding time at different temperatures
Elemental mapping (EDS) to confirm Ag segregation and oxide composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ag-alloyed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both the friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the pure CoCrFeNi samples, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the formation of a continuous, deformable oxide nanocomposite tribolayer, then the hypothesis that Ag addition confers wide-temperature wear protection would be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

Wear-related energy and material loss cost over 2500 Billion Euro per year. Traditional wisdom suggests that high-strength materials reveal low wear rates, yet, their plastic deformation mechanisms also influence their wear performance. High strength and homogeneous deformation behavior, which allow accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture, are crucial for developing wear-resistant metals. Here, we present an approach to achieve superior wear resistance via in-situ formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface during wear, by reaction of the metal surface with its oxidative environment, a principle that we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. We design a TiNbZr-Ag alloy that forms an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer upon dry sliding. The strong (2.4 GPa yield strength) and deformable (homogeneous deformation to 20% strain) nanocomposite surface reduces the wear rate of the TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude.
